text: Your team is integrating a Copilot custom agent that produces draft refactors. Reviewers complain that they can't tell what the agent intended before code changes appear in a PR. Which configuration most directly addresses the complaint?

options.text: Increase the agent's autonomy level so it produces more diff context per PR.
options.why: More diff context is more output, not earlier insight. The complaint is that reviewers cannot see intent before the code exists, and a bigger diff arrives at the same time as the small one.

options.text: Configure the agent to output a structured plan as a workflow artifact before any code changes are written.
options.why: Correct. A structured plan published as a workflow artifact (or PR description) before any code is written is exactly the 'separate planning from execution' pattern. Reviewers validate intent first.

options.text: Require two CODEOWNER approvals on every agent-authored PR.
options.why: CODEOWNERS approvals gate the merge, which happens after the code already exists. It does not surface the agent's intent any earlier.

options.text: Reduce the agent's tool list to read-only operations.
options.why: Making the agent read-only removes the capability entirely instead of making its reasoning visible. That solves the symptom by deleting the feature.

takeaway: Reviewers' complaint is about *visibility before code*. A structured plan artifact published before any change addresses that exactly. CODEOWNER counts (C) gate merge but don't show intent earlier; (A) is opposite of the issue; (D) discards capability.

text: Which of the following is an anti-pattern when integrating an agent into the SDLC? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The agent acts immediately without producing an inspectable plan.
options.why: Correct. 'Planless execution' is the canonical anti-pattern in the Foundations module: the agent starts changing code without an inspectable approach, so reviewers only ever see the diff.

options.text: The agent runs in a workflow with `permissions: { contents: read }`.
options.why: A read-only permissions block is least privilege done right, not an anti-pattern.

options.text: The agent's commit author is the human who triggered the workflow.
options.why: Attribution to the human who triggered the run is acceptable; the anti-pattern is having no attribution or audit trail at all.

options.text: The agent operates on a feature branch protected by branch protection rules.
options.why: Working on a protected feature branch is exactly the bounded, PR-based pattern the modules recommend.

takeaway: Acting without an inspectable plan is the canonical anti-pattern. (B) is fine (read-only is safe), (C) is acceptable when the human triggers it, (D) is good practice.

text: You are designing a "research → propose → apply" agent flow. Which separation produces the most inspectable workflow?

options.text: One job that does all three phases sequentially with grouped logs.
options.why: Grouped logs improve readability but nothing gates the transition from planning to action, so an unreviewed plan still becomes code.

options.text: A planning job that uploads a plan artifact, a reviewer-approved `workflow_dispatch` to begin the action job, then an evaluation job.
options.why: Correct. Plan artifact → human approval → action job → evaluation is the inspectable separation: each phase leaves durable evidence and execution cannot start until the plan is accepted.

options.text: A single job with `if: github.actor == 'admin'` gating the action step.
options.why: Gating on `github.actor` is identity checking, not plan validation. Any admin-triggered run still executes an unreviewed plan.

options.text: Three sequential jobs in the same workflow with `needs:` dependencies.
options.why: `needs:` only enforces ordering. Sequential jobs with no approval gate still run straight through from plan to action.

takeaway: Separation of plan/approve/act/evaluate into discrete artifact-producing steps is the inspectability pattern. (A) groups logs but doesn't gate; (C) is identity gating only; (D) sequential jobs alone don't add approval gates.

text: A regulated team is concerned about agent autonomy. Which design preserves velocity while controlling risk?

options.text: Require human approval on every agent-authored PR regardless of change category.
options.why: Blanket approval on every PR is the 'governance fatigue' failure mode: reviewers rubber-stamp low-risk changes and stop reading the high-risk ones.

options.text: Disable agent access during business hours.
options.why: Time-of-day restrictions do not correlate with risk. A destructive change at 2am is as damaging as one at 2pm.

options.text: Categorize actions by operational/security/compliance risk and require approval only for high-risk categories.
options.why: Correct. Risk-based autonomy — classify by operational, security, and compliance risk, then require approval only where risk is material — is the published guidance in the Governance module.

options.text: Run agents only in a dedicated repository disconnected from production.
options.why: Isolating agents in a scratch repository removes the risk by removing the value. It does not let agents contribute to real work safely.

takeaway: Risk-tiered autonomy is the published guidance. (A) is approval theater; (B)(D) reduce velocity without proportionate safety gain.

text: Which artifact is the most appropriate "inspectable artifact" for an agent's plan in a standard GitHub workflow?

options.text: A console log line in the workflow run.
options.why: Console output scrolls away and is bound to a single run's retention. The modules explicitly recommend uploading artifacts precisely because logs are not durable enough.

options.text: An `actions/upload-artifact`-uploaded JSON or markdown plan document referenced from the PR description.
options.why: Correct. A plan uploaded with `actions/upload-artifact` and linked from an 'Evidence' section in the PR is the canonical GitHub-native inspectable artifact: durable, traceable to a run and commit, reviewable in place.

options.text: An entry in an external Notion database.
options.why: External systems break the 'GitHub as system of record' model — the evidence is no longer attached to the change it justifies.

options.text: A comment in the agent's source code.
options.why: A source comment is not produced per run, so it cannot record what this particular execution intended or did.

takeaway: A workflow artifact referenced from the PR is the canonical inspectable artifact. (A) is ephemeral, (C) is off-platform, (D) isn't an artifact.

text: You want to define success criteria for an agent task that performs a dependency upgrade. Which combination is most robust?

options.text: Tests pass; no new code scanning alerts; PR template required fields completed.
options.why: Correct. Success criteria should be objective and enforceable: required checks pass, no new scanning alerts, and the PR template's required fields are complete. These map directly to status checks the platform can gate on.

options.text: The agent reports "success" in its trace log.
options.why: A self-reported 'success' is the agent grading its own homework. The modules are explicit that evaluation must be grounded in system signals, not agent confidence.

options.text: The PR is opened within 5 minutes of triggering.
options.why: Elapsed time measures speed, not whether the upgrade actually resolved the vulnerability.

options.text: A human approves the PR description.
options.why: Approving the description validates the narrative, not the change. 'CI passed' plus a good story is still not proof the intent was met.

takeaway: Multiple objective criteria mirroring human-contributor judgment. (B) is self-reported, (C) measures speed not quality, (D) is subjective.

text: Your agent occasionally takes actions that contradict its earlier plan. What is the most direct architectural fix?

options.text: Increase the agent's memory window.
options.why: A larger memory window may help the agent remember the plan, but nothing stops it acting when it diverges anyway. This is a hope, not a control.

options.text: Require the agent to re-read and acknowledge its plan artifact at the start of the action phase, and abort if action steps diverge from the plan.
options.why: Correct. Treat the plan as a contract: re-read it at the start of the action phase and abort when steps diverge. Validating plans (and gating action on that validation) is the published Domain 1 skill.

options.text: Switch to a more capable model.
options.why: A more capable model reduces the frequency of divergence but does not detect or block it when it happens.

options.text: Disable retries.
options.why: Retries are about transient failure recovery and are unrelated to plan/action divergence.

takeaway: Plan/action divergence is fixed by making the plan a hard contract, not by upgrading the model or memory.

text: What does an MCP server primarily provide to a Copilot custom agent?

options.text: A vector database for long-term memory.
options.why: Memory is a separate concern (issues, PRs, instructions files). MCP is a tool-exposure protocol, not a memory store.

options.text: A standardized protocol for exposing external tools, APIs, or data sources the agent can invoke.
options.why: Correct. An MCP server exposes tools, APIs, or data sources to an AI client through one standardized protocol, so you do not build a bespoke integration per tool.

options.text: A replacement for GitHub Actions runners.
options.why: Execution still happens on GitHub Actions runners. MCP supplies tools to the agent; it does not host the run.

options.text: A static prompt-template registry.
options.why: MCP describes tools and their invocation, not prompt templates.

takeaway: MCP is the standardized tool-exposure protocol. (A) is wrong (memory is separate), (C) is wrong (MCP doesn't replace runners), (D) is wrong.

text: You configured an MCP server but the agent will not invoke it in your organization. Other agents in the org work fine. Which check should you perform first?

options.text: Confirm the server appears on the organization's MCP allow list.
options.why: Correct. When other agents in the same org work fine, the difference is org-level policy. Check whether 'Restrict MCP access to registry servers' is set to 'Registry only' and whether the server is in the registry.

options.text: Restart the runner.
options.why: Restarting the runner addresses transient infrastructure faults, not a policy block that would fail identically every time.

options.text: Increase the workflow timeout.
options.why: A timeout produces a cancelled run, not a refusal to invoke the server at all.

options.text: Rotate the workflow's `GITHUB_TOKEN`.
options.why: `GITHUB_TOKEN` governs GitHub API access for the workflow, not which MCP servers Copilot policy permits.

takeaway: Allow-list misses are the most common cause when other agents work. Always check the allow list before deeper debugging.

text: What is the purpose of the GitHub remote MCP server?

options.text: To replace local MCP servers with cloud-hosted ones for any vendor.
options.why: 'Remote' describes where the server is hosted, not a universal replacement for every vendor's local server. Local MCP servers remain valid and are required for local-resource access.

options.text: To expose GitHub's own APIs (issues, PRs, code search) to agents through MCP.
options.why: Correct. The GitHub MCP server (hosted at https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/) exposes GitHub's own capabilities — repositories, issues, pull requests, code search — to MCP-capable clients. Remote is the recommended setup for most users in supported IDEs.

options.text: To proxy outbound network calls from the Copilot cloud agent firewall.
options.why: Outbound network control is the job of firewall/egress allow-listing in the agent's execution environment, not of the MCP server.

options.text: To synchronize state between multiple Copilot subscriptions.
options.why: MCP has nothing to do with syncing Copilot subscription state.

takeaway: The GitHub remote MCP server exposes GitHub's APIs as MCP tools.

text: Which of the following statements about MCP allow lists are true? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: MCP allow lists restrict which MCP servers an organization's agents may connect to.
options.why: True. That is precisely their purpose: an org or enterprise policy restricting which MCP servers agents may connect to.

options.text: MCP allow lists set permission levels (read/write) for each MCP tool.
options.why: False. An allow list decides *whether* a server may be used. Read/write capability comes from the tool configuration and the credentials the server is given — not from the allow list.

options.text: Servers not on the allow list are blocked even if explicitly referenced in an agent's config.
options.why: True. Enforcement is at the policy layer. With 'Registry only' selected, a server absent from the registry is blocked even if an agent config names it explicitly — and local servers must be listed with exactly matching IDs.

options.text: MCP allow lists eliminate the need for per-tool permissions in the agent's manifest.
options.why: False. Allow lists and per-tool permissions are complementary layers. Being allowed to reach a server does not grant every tool on it.

takeaway: (a) Yes — that's its purpose. (b) No — permissions live in agent/tool config, not allow lists. (c) Yes — allow lists are enforced regardless of agent intent. (d) No — per-tool permissions still apply within an allowed server.

text: You want a Copilot custom agent to be invoked from a CI workflow when a PR is opened. Which is the most direct configuration?

options.text: Trigger a GitHub Actions workflow on `pull_request: [opened]` with a step that runs the agent.
options.why: Correct. Create a workflow file that triggers on the event (`on: pull_request`), set its `permissions:` block, and run the agent as a step — for example `npx @github/copilot-cli --agent <name> -p "..."`. The workflow becomes the execution boundary.

options.text: Configure a webhook in repository settings to call the agent's HTTP endpoint.
options.why: A webhook to an external endpoint moves execution off-platform, losing the workflow's permission scoping, logs, and artifacts.

options.text: Add the agent to the repository's CODEOWNERS file.
options.why: CODEOWNERS routes review requests. It cannot execute anything.

options.text: Define the agent in `.github/dependabot.yml`.
options.why: `dependabot.yml` configures dependency update PRs only; it does not invoke arbitrary agents.

takeaway: Standard GitHub Actions trigger pattern. (B) is custom plumbing, (C) doesn't run code, (D) is for dependency updates only.

text: Your agent must create branches and pull requests autonomously. Which minimum `permissions:` block in the workflow file is appropriate?

options.text: `permissions: { contents: read, pull-requests: read }`
options.why: Read-only cannot push a branch or open a PR. The workflow would fail at the first write.

options.text: `permissions: { contents: write, pull-requests: write }`
options.why: Correct. `contents: write` allows creating the branch and commits; `pull-requests: write` allows opening and updating the PR. That is the minimum for this task — nothing broader.

options.text: `permissions: write-all`
options.why: `write-all` grants far more than the task needs (packages, deployments, security events, and more) and violates least privilege.

options.text: `permissions: { actions: write }`
options.why: `actions: write` manages workflow runs. It grants neither commit nor PR capability.

takeaway: Minimum needed to create branches and PRs. (A) is read-only, (C) is broader than needed, (D) is for managing workflows.

text: A team wants to allow the Copilot cloud agent to call exactly two external APIs and nothing else. Which control should they configure?

options.text: CODEOWNERS for the agent's branch.
options.why: CODEOWNERS controls who reviews changed paths. It has no effect on outbound network calls.

options.text: The Copilot cloud agent firewall, with an allow list of the two API hosts.
options.why: Correct. Network isolation with an allow list of permitted outbound hosts is the environment-specific constraint control. GitHub Agentic Workflows apply the same defense-in-depth idea: network isolation plus allowlisted outbound access.

options.text: Repository secret scoping.
options.why: Secret scoping controls which credentials a job can read, not which hosts it may reach.

options.text: Branch protection rules on `main`.
options.why: Branch protection governs merges into `main`; it says nothing about egress during a run.

takeaway: The Copilot cloud agent firewall is the named control for egress allow-listing.

text: An agent's tool call to a flaky external service occasionally fails. Which retry strategy is most appropriate?

options.text: Retry up to 10 times immediately on any error.
options.why: Ten immediate retries on any error hammers a struggling service and will happily repeat a logic error ten times, compounding damage.

options.text: Bounded retries with exponential backoff, scoped to transient errors (network, rate-limit), with idempotency keys on the underlying operation.
options.why: Correct. Bounded count, exponential backoff, idempotency on the underlying operation, and retrying only transient classes (network, rate limit) — that is the safe-retry shape the modules describe.

options.text: Retry once, then escalate to a human regardless of error type.
options.why: One retry then escalate is safe but wasteful: it pages a human for an ordinary transient blip that a second attempt would have cleared.

options.text: Disable retries and let the workflow fail.
options.why: Disabling retries turns every transient network hiccup into a failed run and a human interruption.

takeaway: Standard safe-retry pattern: bounded, backoff, idempotency, scoped to transient errors.

text: You need to scope an agent so that it can only modify a single repository, not the entire organization. Which token approach is most aligned with least-privilege?

options.text: A classic personal access token with `repo` scope from the team lead.
options.why: A classic PAT with `repo` scope carries the user's access to *every* repository they can reach — the opposite of repository scoping.

options.text: The workflow's `GITHUB_TOKEN`, which is automatically scoped to that repository.
options.why: Correct. The workflow's `GITHUB_TOKEN` is minted per run and automatically scoped to the repository the workflow lives in, with capability further narrowed by the `permissions:` block.

options.text: A GitHub App installation token granted at the organization level on all repositories.
options.why: An installation token granted org-wide reaches every repository in the installation, which is broader than the task requires.

options.text: An OAuth token from a user with admin rights on all repos.
options.why: An admin user's OAuth token is the widest option available and would let a mistake propagate across the whole organization.

takeaway: `GITHUB_TOKEN` is the textbook least-privilege option for in-repo work. (A) over-scopes by user, (C) over-scopes by org, (D) is far too broad.

text: Which combination provides traceability and accountability for autonomous agent actions in a GitHub workflow?

options.text: Workflow run logs + signed commits attributed to the bot identity + PR comments documenting key decisions.
options.why: Correct. Traceability needs three things together: what happened (run logs), who did it (commit attribution to the agent identity), and why (decisions recorded in the PR). All three live in GitHub and survive the run.

options.text: A single end-of-run summary email to the team.
options.why: An email is a one-time notification, not a durable record attached to the change. You cannot reconstruct a decision trail from an inbox.

options.text: Disabling actions logs to reduce noise.
options.why: Disabling logs removes the primary forensic surface. Missing evidence is treated as a failure in the Governance module.

options.text: Storing the agent's reasoning in a private Slack channel.
options.why: Private chat is off-platform, unattributed to the commit, and typically outside retention and audit policy.

takeaway: The three-pillar pattern: logs, attribution, and decisional comments.

text: Where do long-term, project-stable agent instructions belong?

options.text: Injected into the user prompt each invocation.
options.why: Re-injecting stable facts into every prompt is short-term memory doing long-term memory's job: costly, easy to forget, and invisible to reviewers.

options.text: In `.github/copilot-instructions.md` (or `AGENTS.md`) in the repository.
options.why: Correct. Stable, project-wide guidance belongs in a durable repository artifact such as `.github/copilot-instructions.md` or `AGENTS.md`, where it is versioned, reviewable, and picked up on every invocation.

options.text: In an environment secret.
options.why: Secrets are for credentials. Instructions are not sensitive and secrets are not designed to be read as context.

options.text: Hard-coded into the agent's source binary.
options.why: Hard-coding instructions into a binary makes them unreviewable and unchangeable without a release.

takeaway: Repo-level instructions file is the canonical home for stable long-term agent guidance.

text: An agent is configured to load the entire repository's documentation into its working context every invocation. Performance is poor and answers are diluted. Which adjustment best applies?

options.text: Switch to a larger context window model.
options.why: A bigger context window lets you load more irrelevant text. It raises cost and does not fix dilution.

options.text: Scope memory to task-relevant information only; load only the docs referenced by the current task.
options.why: Correct. 'Scope memory to task-relevant information' is the published skill: load only what affects this task's outcome — requirements, constraints, decisions, validation approach — and leave the rest out.

options.text: Increase retries.
options.why: Retries re-run the same over-loaded context and produce the same diluted answer.

options.text: Disable memory entirely.
options.why: Disabling memory removes the requirements and prior decisions the agent needs. The fix is selectivity, not amnesia.

takeaway: Scope memory to task-relevant — published Domain 3 bullet. Bigger windows and more retries don't fix dilution.

text: An agent is mid-task when its workflow run is canceled. On the next invocation, you need it to resume without repeating completed steps. What pattern enables this?

options.text: Increase the workflow `timeout-minutes`.
options.why: A longer timeout reduces how often the run is cut short but does nothing to make the next run resume rather than restart.

options.text: Persist task progress as a durable artifact (PR checklist, state file, or issue comments), and have the agent read it at the start of each run to skip completed steps.
options.why: Correct. Durable state — PR description checkboxes, commits already pushed, workflow run results in the Checks tab — lets the agent open the existing PR, see what is done, and continue from the latest state.

options.text: Set `concurrency: { group: agent-task, cancel-in-progress: false }`.
options.why: Concurrency settings control whether runs overlap or cancel each other. They do not carry progress between runs.

options.text: Use a larger runner.
options.why: Runner size affects speed, not the ability to resume from persisted state.

takeaway: Durable progress artifact pattern is the published resumption mechanism.

text: Which of the following describes context drift in an extended agent execution?

options.text: The agent's responses become slower over time as memory grows.
options.why: Slower responses are a performance symptom. Drift is about correctness of alignment, not latency.

options.text: The agent acts on cached or stale context that no longer matches the actual repo state.
options.why: Correct. Context drift is when the agent's actions no longer align with the original goal or prior decisions — typically because it is working from stale or cached context rather than current repository state.

options.text: The agent's prompt template becomes too long.
options.why: A long prompt template is a cost and context-budget problem, not drift.

options.text: The workflow run consumes too much GitHub Actions quota.
options.why: Actions minutes consumption is a billing concern, unrelated to alignment.

takeaway: Context drift specifically = action-state divergence; the others are unrelated performance/scale issues.

text: Two agents in a workflow each maintain their own local state and reach conflicting conclusions about the current branch state. What's the fix?

options.text: Give one agent priority over the other.
options.why: Priority rules pick a winner without making the two views consistent. The losing agent still holds a wrong picture of the world.

options.text: Use a single canonical state artifact that both agents read and update through serialized writes.
options.why: Correct. Define a single source of truth per information type and serialize writes to it. In GitHub that means the issue holds requirements and the PR holds decisions and progress — every tool reads and updates the same artifact rather than keeping private copies.

options.text: Run the agents in different repositories.
options.why: Separate repositories eliminate the collision by eliminating the collaboration. The agents still need shared state.

options.text: Reduce both agents' memory to short-term only.
options.why: Shrinking memory does not stop two agents from independently forming conflicting private views.

takeaway: Single source of truth + serialized writes is the canonical fix.

text: Which of the following are automated evaluation signals you should configure for an agent's output? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Code scanning (CodeQL) alerts.
options.why: Automated. Code scanning (CodeQL) produces alerts and check runs without human involvement.

options.text: Secret scanning results.
options.why: Automated. Secret scanning — and push protection — generate signals mechanically.

options.text: Dependabot dependency review.
options.why: Automated. Dependency review runs as a check on the PR and blocks known-vulnerable dependencies.

options.text: Reviewer commentary in PR threads.
options.why: Not automated. Reviewer commentary is a qualitative human signal. It matters for evaluation, but the question asks specifically about automated scanning signals.

takeaway: All three are automated scanners. (D) is human input, not automated.

text: An agent's PRs frequently pass tests but introduce performance regressions on a critical path. The team wants this caught automatically before merge. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Ask reviewers to read every diff carefully.
options.why: Asking humans to read more carefully is a process wish, not an enforceable control. It fails exactly when the team is busy.

options.text: Add a performance benchmark step that produces a required status check; fail the check if regression exceeds threshold.
options.why: Correct. Turn the operational constraint into a machine-checkable signal: run the benchmark in CI, fail the job past a threshold, and make it a required status check so a regressing PR cannot merge.

options.text: Disable the agent for critical-path files.
options.why: Blocking the agent from critical-path files removes capability instead of adding a gate, and humans regress performance too.

options.text: Increase test timeout values.
options.why: Raising test timeouts hides the regression by making the slow code pass.

takeaway: Required status check on a benchmark is the standard gate. (A) doesn't scale, (C) over-restricts, (D) hides the regression.

text: An agent's failure trace shows that it called the wrong tool for a task. Which root-cause category does this most closely match?

options.text: Reasoning error.
options.why: A reasoning error is a wrong plan or wrong inference — misreading requirements, choosing invalid logic. Here the plan may have been fine; the execution reached for the wrong instrument.

options.text: Tool misuse.
options.why: Correct. Tool misuse covers calling the wrong tool, or calling the right tool incorrectly — misconfigured workflows, wrong commands, failing to trigger a workflow properly.

options.text: Context or environment issue.
options.why: Context issues are missing, stale, or conflicting information. Nothing in the trace points to bad inputs.

options.text: Network failure.
options.why: A network failure is an environment fault, not a decision the agent made.

takeaway: Wrong tool call = tool misuse by definition.

text: After analyzing failures, you find that the agent consistently misinterprets a custom internal API because its description in the agent's config is ambiguous. What is the most appropriate tuning step?

options.text: Revise the agent's tool descriptions and add usage examples in its config.
options.why: Correct. When the root cause is an ambiguous tool description, the fix is to refine tool usage and access: clarify the description, add usage examples, and rename anything ambiguous.

options.text: Increase the agent's max-token budget.
options.why: A larger token budget does not disambiguate a description the model is reading correctly and interpreting reasonably.

options.text: Remove the tool from the agent's available list.
options.why: Removing the tool discards capability the agent legitimately needs. Tune before you amputate.

options.text: Switch to a different LLM provider.
options.why: Changing model provider is an expensive shot in the dark for a problem you have already localized to your own configuration.

takeaway: Tune by revising tool descriptions/examples. (B)(D) are unrelated; (C) discards capability.

text: Which of the following best aligns evaluation criteria with development intent?

options.text: Use eval signals that mirror the criteria a human contributor would be judged on (tests, scans, review feedback).
options.why: Correct. Aligning evaluation with development intent means judging agent work by the same signals a human contributor is judged on — tests, lint, security scans, review feedback — so agents stay accountable to the team's real quality bar.

options.text: Define agent-only metrics like "tool calls per task" as the primary success measure.
options.why: Agent-only metrics such as tool calls per task measure mechanism, not outcome. Optimizing them can actively diverge from what the team wants.

options.text: Disable code review for agent-authored PRs to measure raw agent capability.
options.why: Removing review from agent PRs breaks the contributor model and deletes the qualitative signal.

options.text: Use only the LLM's self-reported confidence score.
options.why: Self-reported confidence is the one signal the modules explicitly warn against: evaluation must be grounded in system signals, not the agent's confidence.

takeaway: Alignment with contributor judgment criteria is the published principle.

text: Which artifacts are most useful when diagnosing a failed agent run? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Workflow run logs.
options.why: Yes. Workflow run logs show what executed and where it errored.

options.text: The agent's structured plan output.
options.why: Yes. The structured plan captures intent, so you can compare what was supposed to happen with what did.

options.text: The execution trace (tool calls in order).
options.why: Yes. The execution trace shows the ordered tool calls, which is how you spot tool misuse.

options.text: The uploaded artifacts (intermediate state, evaluations).
options.why: Yes. Uploaded artifacts hold intermediate state and evaluation output, and remain available after logs scroll away. All four are named diagnostic surfaces.

takeaway: All four are the listed diagnostic surfaces.

text: An agent's reasoning is consistently wrong about the team's preferred coding style. Which tuning is most direct?

options.text: Update the agent's custom instructions in `.github/copilot-instructions.md` with the team's style conventions.
options.why: Correct. Team conventions are stable, project-wide knowledge, so they belong in repository instructions. Revising instructions is the first tuning lever for reasoning errors.

options.text: Increase the agent's autonomy level.
options.why: Raising autonomy lets the agent apply the wrong style faster and with less oversight.

options.text: Add a `style-check` retry loop.
options.why: A retry loop re-runs the same misunderstanding; it treats a knowledge gap as a transient fault.

options.text: Reduce the agent's memory.
options.why: Reducing memory removes context. The problem is that the correct convention was never recorded anywhere durable.

takeaway: Custom instructions are the canonical home for team conventions.

text: Which pattern best describes a "supervisor" multi-agent orchestration?

options.text: All agents act simultaneously and outputs are merged at the end.
options.why: Simultaneous execution with a merge at the end is fan-out/fan-in — in GitHub Actions, parallel jobs plus a `needs:` job that fans in.

options.text: One agent dispatches sub-tasks to worker agents and reviews their outputs.
options.why: Correct. In the supervisor pattern one agent dispatches sub-tasks to workers and reviews their outputs, holding responsibility for allocation and acceptance.

options.text: Two agents debate and a third arbitrates.
options.why: Two agents arguing with a third arbitrating is the debate/critic pattern, used to resolve contradictory outputs.

options.text: Agents are arranged in a fixed sequential pipeline.
options.why: A fixed ordered chain is the sequential pipeline pattern (planner → coder → reviewer).

takeaway: Supervisor = dispatch + review. (A) is fan-out/fan-in, (C) is debate/critic, (D) is sequential pipeline.

text: You run three agents in parallel on the same repository. To prevent conflicting code changes, which approach is best?

options.text: Run all three agents against the `main` branch directly.
options.why: Three agents writing to `main` share one execution context — interleaved commits, ambiguous ownership, and no PR boundary to review at.

options.text: Run each agent on its own feature branch with non-overlapping file scopes, and detect conflicts at PR-merge time.
options.why: Correct. Isolation is the precondition for safe parallelism: a dedicated branch per agent (`agent/dependency/<ticket>`), non-overlapping path scopes, and conflict detection at the PR layer.

options.text: Disable two of the agents and run them sequentially.
options.why: Serializing works but throws away the throughput you wanted. Isolation lets you keep the parallelism.

options.text: Increase the runner size to handle merges.
options.why: Runner size is a performance dial and has no bearing on whether two agents collide on the same file.

takeaway: Branch isolation + file-scope separation + PR-time conflict detection is the parallel-agent pattern.

text: Two parallel agents produce contradictory PRs that modify the same file. Which recovery pattern is most appropriate?

options.text: Auto-merge both PRs.
options.why: Auto-merging both guarantees the semantic conflict lands in `main`, where it is most expensive to unpick.

options.text: A reconciler (judge agent) with a defined arbitration rule, or human-in-the-loop review if disagreement exceeds threshold.
options.why: Correct. Resolve conflicts intentionally: a reconciler with a defined arbitration rule, or human-in-the-loop review once disagreement passes a threshold. Without arbitration, whichever PR merges first simply wins by timing.

options.text: Reject both PRs without review.
options.why: Rejecting both discards work and does not decide which approach was right.

options.text: Force-push to overwrite one of the branches.
options.why: A force-push destroys one agent's history and its audit trail, and still leaves the conflict undecided.

takeaway: Reconciler agent or human-in-the-loop is the published recovery pattern.

text: Which artifact best supports post-hoc analysis of a multi-agent workflow?

options.text: A top-level orchestration record (issue or workflow run) linking every sub-agent's run, with decision logs at handoffs.
options.why: Correct. Post-hoc analysis needs a linked record: a top-level orchestration artifact tying every sub-agent run together with decisions logged at each handoff, so you can replay who did what and why.

options.text: A summary log message on the orchestrator's exit.
options.why: A single exit summary tells you the ending, not the sequence of decisions that produced it.

options.text: Each agent's local debug output, kept only on its runner.
options.why: Debug output kept on the runner is discarded with the runner. Nothing durable survives.

options.text: A Slack thread between the team's engineers.
options.why: A Slack thread is off-platform, unattributed to runs and commits, and outside retention policy.

takeaway: Linked orchestration record with handoff logs is the auditable structure.

text: Your orchestrator detects that one of three parallel agents has produced no progress for 30 minutes. What's the most appropriate first response?

options.text: Allow the agent to continue indefinitely.
options.why: Letting a stalled agent run indefinitely burns budget and blocks downstream fan-in jobs forever.

options.text: Apply a workflow timeout, mark the run failed, and route the sub-task to a fallback path (rerun, alternative agent, or human).
options.why: Correct. Detect the stall with `timeout-minutes`, mark it failed, and route to a fallback: rerun the sub-agent in isolation, use an alternative, or escalate to a human with a concise summary.

options.text: Increase the runner's CPU allocation.
options.why: More CPU does not help an agent that is stuck rather than slow.

options.text: Cancel all three agents' runs.
options.why: Cancelling all three throws away the two runs that are working fine.

takeaway: Timeout + fallback path is the standard stalled-execution response.

text: You want to introduce a new agent into an existing multi-agent workflow without disrupting current runs. Which deployment is safest?

options.text: Replace the existing agent immediately and roll forward.
options.why: An immediate swap changes behavior for in-flight work with no evidence that the replacement is equivalent.

options.text: Deploy the new agent in shadow mode, run it alongside the existing one, compare outputs, then promote once parity is confirmed.
options.why: Correct. Shadow mode — run the new agent alongside the incumbent, compare outputs, grant no merge authority until parity is confirmed — adds the agent without disrupting active workflows.

options.text: Run the new agent only on weekends.
options.why: Weekend-only scheduling limits exposure by clock time, not by risk, and gives you a thin, unrepresentative sample.

options.text: Disable the existing agent for one week to validate the new one.
options.why: Disabling the incumbent for a week removes the baseline you need to compare against, and leaves no fallback if the new agent misbehaves.

takeaway: Shadow-mode parity check is the safe rollout.

text: A retired agent's audit trail must remain accessible for compliance review. Which approach preserves auditability?

options.text: Delete the agent's config and all associated workflow runs.
options.why: Deleting configuration and runs destroys exactly the evidence compliance review depends on. Note that deleted workflow artifacts cannot be restored.

options.text: Archive the config in git history, retain workflow runs/artifacts per retention policy, and document the retirement in a governance record.
options.why: Correct. Retire while preserving auditability: the config stays in git history, runs and artifacts are retained under the retention policy, and the retirement decision is documented in a governance record.

options.text: Move the workflow runs to a private external storage system not linked to the repository.
options.why: Moving runs to unlinked external storage severs evidence from the changes it explains and usually falls outside the audit log.

options.text: Disable workflow logging going forward.
options.why: Disabling logging protects nothing about the past and destroys the trail going forward.

takeaway: Archive in git + retain runs + document = audit-trail preservation.

text: Which action category most clearly requires explicit human authorization?

options.text: Auto-formatting a markdown file.
options.why: Formatting a markdown file is the low-risk, fully reversible tier — a candidate for full automation.

options.text: Renaming a private variable in test code.
options.why: Renaming a private variable in test code is contained and reversible; PR plus required checks is proportionate.

options.text: Modifying a CI/CD pipeline that deploys to production.
options.why: Correct. Changes under `.github/workflows/` that deploy to production are the classic 'small diff, big consequence' area — treat as high or critical risk and require explicit human authorization.

options.text: Adding a comment to an existing issue.
options.why: Commenting on an issue changes no code and no system state.

takeaway: Production CI/CD changes are explicitly the high-risk category.

text: Which mechanism most directly enforces least-privilege execution context for an agent in a workflow?

options.text: A workflow `permissions:` block scoped to the minimum needed for the task.
options.why: Correct. The `permissions:` block is the platform primitive for least privilege at execution time. Default to `contents: read` at workflow level and elevate only on the job that must write.

options.text: A team-wide announcement in Slack.
options.why: A Slack announcement is documentation of intent, not a technical control. The Governance module is blunt: if the platform cannot enforce it, it will be bypassed.

options.text: A pinned issue describing expected behavior.
options.why: A pinned issue describes expected behavior. It cannot constrain a token.

options.text: A README note in the repository root.
options.why: A README note is 'controls in docs only' — the named anti-pattern.

takeaway: Workflow `permissions:` block is the GitHub primitive for least privilege at execution time.

text: You want to require approval before an agent can deploy to production but not for routine PRs. Which GitHub feature is most appropriate?

options.text: Branch protection rules on `main`.
options.why: Branch protection on `main` gates merges. It does not gate what happens at deploy time, and it would add friction to every routine PR.

options.text: An environment with required reviewers attached to the production deploy job.
options.why: Correct. An environment with required reviewers pauses the deploy job until a human approves, and can restrict production secrets to that environment — targeted oversight exactly at the high-impact decision point.

options.text: CODEOWNERS for the entire `src/` directory.
options.why: CODEOWNERS on all of `src/` taxes every ordinary change while still not gating the deployment itself.

options.text: A `WORKING-HOURS` setting on the repository.
options.why: There is no such repository setting.

takeaway: Environment protection rules with required reviewers are the named gate for deploys.

text: Which of the following minimize approval friction without reducing safety? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Require approval only for irreversible or compliance-sensitive changes.
options.why: Yes. Requiring approval only where changes are irreversible or compliance-sensitive concentrates human attention where it buys real safety.

options.text: Use CODEOWNERS on sensitive paths so reviews are targeted, not global.
options.why: Yes. Path-scoped CODEOWNERS routes review to people with context instead of taxing everyone on everything.

options.text: Require two reviewers on every PR including doc typos.
options.why: No. Two reviewers on a documentation typo is approval theater: it adds friction and trains reviewers to stop reading.

options.text: Use environment protection rules so prod deploys are gated but dev flows freely.
options.why: Yes. Environment protection rules gate production while dev and staging flow freely — velocity preserved, risk still gated.

takeaway: All target risk-proportionate approval; (C) is approval theater that adds friction without proportionate safety.

text: An agent is about to perform an irreversible production change (e.g., dropping a database column). Which set of controls is the best combination?

options.text: CODEOWNERS approval on the migration file + environment protection rule with required reviewers on the prod environment + a structured plan artifact reviewed before the action job runs.
options.why: Correct. Defense in depth for an irreversible change: CODEOWNERS review of the migration itself, an environment gate with required reviewers at the deploy, and a plan artifact reviewed before the action job runs. Layered controls, each catching what the others miss.

options.text: A retry loop with exponential backoff.
options.why: A retry loop makes an irreversible destructive operation happen repeatedly. This is the worst possible answer here.

options.text: A larger workflow `timeout-minutes` value.
options.why: A longer timeout gives the destructive operation more time to complete. It adds no oversight.

options.text: Allow the agent to proceed and revert later if needed.
options.why: 'Revert later' does not apply to irreversible changes — a dropped column takes the data with it.

takeaway: Defense-in-depth: code-level review (CODEOWNERS) + deploy-gate (environment) + intent review (plan artifact).
